scope: Claim-level trichome morphology, cannabinoid biosynthesis, cannabinoid transformation, developmental, sampling, and analytical evidence for THC-ENC-221 through THC-ENC-240.
rules: Direct cannabis-specific evidence is preferred for trichome morphology, pathway enzymes, chemotype genetics, and analytical behavior.
Engineered or in-vitro pathway evidence establishes biochemical capability but is not treated as a cultivation-rate or potency prescription.
Visual trichome observations are not treated as direct cannabinoid assays unless paired with validated local chemistry.
Claim mapping does not approve a lesson, visual, assessment rationale, or publication state.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis glandular trichomes undergo developmentally and genotype-dependent changes in morphology, and their secretory cells differentiate specialized structural compartments rather than remaining static epidermal structures.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja et al. 2023 microscopy and developmental observations; Livingston et al. 2022 ultrastructural localization of specialized secretory-cell architecture.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports developmental and structural language for glandular trichome initiation and maturation.
claimEvidence.limitations: The cited work examines specific genotypes, tissues, and developmental stages and does not establish one universal trichome-development timeline.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Bulbous glandular trichomes are a recognized small glandular trichome form in cannabis, but morphology alone does not establish their quantitative contribution to whole-flower cannabinoid content.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja et al. 2023 microscopy and trichome-type observations.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports bulbous-trichome classification while preventing potency inference from morphology alone.
claimEvidence.limitations: Chemical contribution of bulbous trichomes to whole-flower cannabinoid abundance is not established by morphology-only evidence.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Capitate-sessile glandular trichomes occur on cannabis reproductive tissues and their relative abundance and morphology can change with developmental stage and genotype.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja et al. 2023 developmental microscopy across flowering.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports sessile-trichome morphology and developmental variability.
claimEvidence.limitations: Not every sessile gland should be assumed to mature into a stalked gland, and classification can vary with sampling and imaging.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Capitate-stalked trichomes contain specialized secretory cells associated with an extracellular storage cavity, and mature glandular heads show developmentally changing morphology.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja et al. 2023 microscopy; Livingston et al. 2022 ultrastructure and enzyme localization.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports stalked-trichome structural and secretory-compartment descriptions.
claimEvidence.limitations: Structure and presence of a gland do not by themselves quantify cannabinoid concentration or whole-plant yield.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis glandular trichome secretory cells are highly polarized, with pathway components compartmentalized across plastids, ER-associated membranes, the cell surface, and the extracellular storage cavity.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Livingston et al. 2022 cryofixation, quantitative electron microscopy, and immunogold labeling.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports secretory-disk-cell and storage-cavity compartmentation language.
claimEvidence.limitations: The study supports a compartmentation model but does not resolve every transport intermediate or membrane-transfer mechanism.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Trichome and cannabinoid measurements are sensitive to tissue position, developmental stage, genotype, and sampling method, so density or chemistry comparisons require a defined sampling frame.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja et al. 2023 trichome-development variability; Namdar et al. 2018 inflorescence-position and method-dependent chemistry.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports standardized trichome-density and chemistry sampling rather than convenience images or arbitrary flower positions.
claimEvidence.limitations: The direction and magnitude of positional gradients can differ among genotypes and production systems.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Hexanoyl-CoA is an established upstream precursor for the polyketide branch of cannabinoid biosynthesis in cannabis trichomes, while the prenyl branch supplies geranyl diphosphate.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Stout et al. 2012 biochemical and expression evidence; Livingston et al. 2022 pathway compartmentation.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the mixed-origin precursor model for major pentyl cannabinoid biosynthesis.
claimEvidence.limitations: Pathway precursor identity does not establish a cultivation input that proportionally increases cannabinoid yield.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis olivetolic acid formation requires tetraketide synthase together with olivetolic acid cyclase, which directs cyclization of the linear polyketide intermediate to olivetolic acid.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Gagne et al. 2012 biochemical characterization and trichome expression evidence.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the enzymatic route to olivetolic acid.
claimEvidence.limitations: In-vitro enzyme chemistry does not quantify intact-plant flux control or prove which cultivation variables limit the pathway.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Reconstructed cannabinoid biosynthesis confirms CBGA formation from the olivetolic-acid and geranyl-diphosphate branches and places CBGA upstream of several major cannabinoid-acid products.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Luo et al. 2019 reconstructed biosynthesis and functional prenyltransferase work.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports CBGA as a major shared precursor in the canonical pathway.
claimEvidence.limitations: The engineered-yeast system demonstrates pathway capability but does not define flux or abundance in intact cannabis flowers.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Functional THCA synthase catalyzes oxidative cyclization of CBGA to THCA, while the genomic region containing cannabinoid-acid synthase loci is structurally complex.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Sirikantaramas et al. 2004 cloning and heterologous expression; Grassa et al. 2018 genomic mapping.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the enzyme-substrate relationship and cautions against simplistic genotype interpretation.
claimEvidence.limitations: Presence or similarity of a synthase sequence does not by itself establish functional enzyme activity or measured flower chemotype.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Recombinant CBDA synthase converts CBGA to CBDA and is closely related to THCA synthase, while chemotype-associated synthase loci occur in a structurally complex genomic region.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Taura et al. 2007 biochemical characterization; Grassa et al. 2018 locus mapping.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports CBDAS function and separates enzyme identity from whole-plant chemical measurement.
claimEvidence.limitations: CBDAS genotype does not by itself quantify absolute CBDA/CBD concentration or prove absence of other cannabinoid acids.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis genomic and functional mapping identified CBCAS activity within the cannabinoid oxidocyclase family, supporting CBCA as a biosynthetic product rather than merely an analytical artifact.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Grassa et al. 2018 physical/genetic map and CBCAS characterization.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports a dedicated CBCA-forming pathway within the oxidocyclase family.
claimEvidence.limitations: Minor-product abundance and enzyme specificity can vary, so pathway presence does not establish a universal CBCA concentration.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Propyl-side-chain cannabinoids can arise from alternate precursor use, and C3/C5 cannabinoid composition shows non-simple inheritance in a studied cannabis F2 population.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Luo et al. 2019 reconstructed pentyl/varin pathways; Welling et al. 2019 segregation analysis.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports varin cannabinoids as alternate biosynthetic branches rather than degradation products of pentyl cannabinoids.
claimEvidence.limitations: Inheritance observed in one population should not be generalized as a universal Mendelian ratio.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Acidic cannabinoids and their neutral counterparts are chemically distinct analytes, and controlled heating can convert acidic forms toward neutral forms through decarboxylation.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Wang et al. 2016 controlled decarboxylation study.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports separate reporting of acidic and neutral cannabinoids and method-aware interpretation.
claimEvidence.limitations: Observed acid/neutral ratios depend on sample history and analytical method and should not be treated as fixed cultivar constants.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabinoid-acid decarboxylation is time- and temperature-dependent under controlled analytical conditions and differs among cannabinoid acids.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Wang et al. 2016 kinetic decarboxylation experiments.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports reaction-specific, condition-dependent decarboxylation chemistry.
claimEvidence.limitations: The tested laboratory conditions do not define one universal operational processing schedule for plant material.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis phytocannabinoid profiles change after harvest as a function of storage duration, temperature, sample form, and matrix, demonstrating that postharvest chemistry is dynamic.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Milay et al. 2020 one-year controlled storage study.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports oxidation/degradation and storage-change boundaries.
claimEvidence.limitations: The study covers selected chemovars, matrices, and conditions and does not establish one degradation rate for all cannabis products.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabinoid phenotype reflects genetic pathway architecture but measured concentration also varies with tissue position and production context, so genotype and environment should not be collapsed into one explanation.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Grassa et al. 2018 genetic architecture; Namdar et al. 2018 position- and method-dependent chemistry.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports separating chemotype genetics from absolute concentration and sampling effects.
claimEvidence.limitations: These sources do not quantify the complete genotype-by-environment response surface for all cultivars.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis trichome morphology changes across flower development, while measured cannabinoid composition also varies by inflorescence position and sampling method, making developmental comparisons dependent on standardized sampling.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja et al. 2023 developmental trichome study; Namdar et al. 2018 spatial chemistry study.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports developmental-stage records and repeated, position-controlled sampling.
claimEvidence.limitations: The sources do not justify a universal harvest week or a single morphology-based chemical optimum.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Visible trichome color and senescence can change during maturation and postharvest handling, while cannabinoid chemistry also changes with storage; color therefore cannot be treated as a direct quantitative cannabinoid assay.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja et al. 2023 trichome maturation observations; Milay et al. 2020 postharvest chemistry.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports using trichome color only as a field observation unless locally validated against chemistry.
claimEvidence.limitations: No universal color threshold is established for potency, cannabinoid ratio, or harvest timing.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis inflorescence is chemically heterogeneous, so laboratory results support batch-level claims only to the extent that sampling, identity, preparation, analytical method, and reporting basis are fit for purpose.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Sarma et al. 2020 USP expert-panel quality review; Namdar et al. 2018 position/method variability.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports representative sampling and claims discipline for cannabinoid testing.
claimEvidence.limitations: A laboratory result describes the submitted sample and method and cannot prove exact composition of every unit in a heterogeneous batch.
